name: recipient-list
intent: Route a message to a set of recipients that is computed at runtime from data - configuration, message content or a registry - instead of being fixed in the routing code, by forwarding a copy of the message to every channel in the computed list.
problem: The set of receivers a message must reach is not static: it depends on message content, tenant, subscription data or an operational roster. Hard-coding the receivers (or a chain of if-statements that mirrors the list) makes every membership change a code change and a redeployment of the router, and couples the producer to consumers it should not know.
context: Message-oriented middleware and in-process messaging where one inbound message must reach several endpoints and where the membership of that set is owned by data (subscription table, tenant registry, on-call roster, supplier list). It applies when the sender must stay decoupled from who receives the message, when a recipient may be added or removed without touching the routing code, and when per-recipient failure is acceptable or handled explicitly rather than atomically.
benefits: Recipient membership becomes data: adding, removing or time-boxing a recipient is a configuration or registry change, not a code change and redeploy of the router.
The sender stays decoupled: it addresses a channel and never learns how many or which endpoints actually received the message.
One message can serve several consumers without the sender orchestrating them; computing the set and traversing it are the router's job.
Recipient computation is isolated, so it is testable as a pure message-to-list decision independent of delivery.
The same router serves one-recipient and many-recipient cases, so a policy change ('also notify finance this quarter') needs no new code path.
Pairs naturally with reply-side patterns: fan-out plus an Aggregator or Scatter-Gather turns notification into request-and-merge without rewriting the router.
tradeoffs: The set of consumers is invisible in the code: dependency discovery and impact analysis require access to the recipient data source, and a stale registry entry silently misroutes traffic.
Fan-out multiplies load and message copies - N recipients mean N copies - so large payloads should move by claim check instead of being copied N times.
Delivery is not atomic: one inbound message becomes N independent sends, so partial delivery is the normal outcome and receivers need idempotency or deduplication.
A sequential traversal lets one slow, blocked or dead recipient delay - or, without a timeout, stall - delivery to all the remaining recipients.
When the recipient list is taken from the message itself, the message author controls the destinations; an unvalidated list is a routing-injection and data-exfiltration surface.
Debugging changes character: 'who received this message?' is no longer readable from the code, so message history or a wire tap is needed to answer it after the fact.
The pattern has no reply aggregation of its own; combining the recipients' answers requires an Aggregator or Scatter-Gather layered on top.

participants.responsibility: Inspects the incoming message, asks the recipient computation for the target set, traverses it and forwards a copy of the message to each recipient channel; it does not process the message itself.
Derives the recipient set for this message from content, configuration or a directory; conceptually separate from the traversal even when one component implements both.
One channel per potential receiver; every channel in the computed list receives its own copy of the message.
Holds the changeable data behind the list (subscriptions, tenant or roster entries) so that membership changes never touch the routing code.
Delivers each copy to its channel, providing the addressing, buffering and - where present - the durability that the router relies on.
Decides what happens when a send fails or times out: abort the fan-out or continue with the remaining recipients, and whether the outcome is reported or aggregated.

use_cases: Credit assessment: a small order routes to one agency, a large order to several agencies whose results are compared - the list is computed from the order value.
Request for quote: an RFQ is sent to a selected set of suppliers held per product category or user preference rather than to every vendor.
Domain event distribution: an order event reaches billing, inventory and analytics, with the per-event subscriptions held in configuration instead of wired in code.
Notification fan-out: an alert reaches the on-call roster resolved at send time, so shift changes need no redeployment.
Multi-tenant delivery: an inbound message is copied to the tenant-specific queues resolved from a tenant registry.
Regulatory reporting: the same transaction message is sent to every jurisdiction-specific reporter listed in a maintained data set.
Apache Camel route: the Recipient List EIP evaluates an expression or header into endpoint URIs for each exchange, then sends sequentially or with configured parallel processing and failure handling.

Spring Integration flow: RecipientListRouter dispatches one message to multiple channels and can use dynamically selected recipients; use a Publish-Subscribe Channel instead when subscription ownership, not per-message selection, is the requirement.
Red Hat Fuse (Apache Camel) route: the recipientList processor computes destinations at runtime for each incoming message, making partner or tenant fan-out data-driven rather than hard-coded.
avoid_when: Every interested consumer must receive the message: a Publish-Subscribe Channel is the better fit, because there the subscriptions themselves are the data.
The route selects exactly one destination from the message content: use a Content-Based Router or Message Router instead.
Recipients are effectively fixed at design time and never change: a static list in code - or plain method calls in-process - is simpler than a routing abstraction.
The message must visit destinations in a defined order or follow per-message steps: use a Routing Slip or Process Manager; a recipient list is unordered fan-out, not a pipeline.
The sender must collect and merge the answers: reach for Scatter-Gather with an Aggregator rather than fanning out and re-inventing reply correlation by hand.
anti_patterns: Taking the recipient list from the message payload without validation, so any producer can direct the message to arbitrary destinations - a routing-injection and exfiltration vector.
Emulating publish-subscribe with a recipient list: recomputing subscribers per message when the platform already offers subscription-driven channels.
Unbounded sequential fan-out with no per-send timeout, so one dead or slow recipient serialises the router for every message behind it.
Mutating the shared message between sends, so later recipients observe unintended content changes; the pattern forwards a copy, not a half-updated original.

Re-implementing the recipient list inside a framework that already provides it (Camel recipientList, Spring Integration RecipientListRouter) and thereby bypassing its timeout, failure and management handling.
design_principles: Declarative configuration over hard-coded structure: recipient membership is data, which keeps the router closed for modification.
Loose coupling: the sender addresses a channel, never a receiver, so the recipient set can change without touching the producer.
Separation of concerns: computing the recipients and delivering to them are two responsibilities even when one component implements both.
Least privilege for dynamic input: externally supplied recipient values must be validated against an allow-list before they can steer the message.
Design for partial failure: N independent sends imply at-least-once delivery per recipient, so idempotency is part of the contract.
best_practices: Keep recipient computation separate from the traversal and test it as a message-to-list function.
Validate computed recipients against an allow-list (known channels, permitted schemes, tenant scope) before any send.
Define the per-recipient failure policy explicitly - fail-fast versus continue - with a send timeout and a report of what actually went out.
Bound the fan-out: cap the recipient count and the delivery parallelism so a large or hostile list cannot exhaust threads or connections.
Send a fresh copy to each recipient and keep the original message immutable during the fan-out.
Make receivers idempotent (see Idempotent Receiver), because a partial retry after a failed fan-out is the normal failure mode.
Publish the computed recipient set to message history or a wire tap so dynamic routing stays observable.
Prefer a Publish-Subscribe Channel when membership is subscription data; use a recipient list when the producer must compute the set per message.
sources: Hohpe & Woolf, Enterprise Integration Patterns: Designing, Building, and Deploying Messaging Solutions (Addison-Wesley, 2003) - Recipient List (Message Routing chapter; compute the recipient set, then forward a copy to each channel).
